title: Why people in the capital say yes
translation: Gyōren, the priest at the Hidenin charity house, was born into the Miura family, I believe, and had once been a warrior without equal. One day someone from his home in the east came to see him, and as they talked the visitor said: "When people from the east say they'll do something, you can count on it. People in the capital are very good at saying yes, but there's nothing behind it."

"I can see why you'd think so," said the priest. "But I've lived in the capital a long time, I know them well now, and I don't think they're worse people. They're gentle and kind, all of them, so when someone asks for something, they can't bring themselves to say no outright. They can't turn anything down. They're soft, and they say yes. They don't mean to lie. But they're all poor and can't do much, so naturally a lot of what they mean to do never happens. The eastern people are my own people, but to be honest, they have no gentleness and not much feeling. They're blunt through and through, so they say no from the start, and that's the end of it. And they're well off, so of course people can count on them."

He put it so clearly. This priest had a heavy accent and a rough way of talking, and I'd thought he probably didn't understand the finer points of the scriptures. After that one remark I thought much more of him. Out of so many priests, he was the one put in charge of a temple, and I thought this was why: he had this gentleness in him, and it did people good.

literal: Holy Man Gyōren of Hidenin was, by his lay family name, someone of the Miura, I think, a peerless warrior.

A person from his home region came and was talking, and said, 'It is the people of the east whose word can be relied on. People of the capital are only good at saying yes, and there is no truth in it', to which
the holy man said: 'You may well think so, but I have lived in the capital a long time and, being used to them, I see that I do not think people's hearts are inferior.
Because they are generally soft-hearted and have feeling, what people ask of them they find it hard to refuse flatly, they cannot say no to anything, and weakly they say yes.
They do not mean to deceive, but since they are all poor and unable to manage, naturally there must be many cases where their intentions are not carried through.
The people of the east are my own side, but in truth they have no tenderness of heart, they are lacking in feeling, and they are wholly blunt, so they say no from the start and that is the end of it.
Since they are prosperous and rich, people rely on them.' That he explained it so,
this holy man, whose speech was crooked and rough, (I had) thought he might not understand the fine principles of the sacred teachings at all, but after this one remark he became admirable, and
I felt that, among so many, his being made head of a temple was because he had such gentleness, and that it was of benefit too.

notes.text: {悲田院|ひでんゐん}: a Buddhist charity house in Kyoto that took in the sick, the poor and orphans (the 1925 edition places it west of the Kamo River). The name comes from the Buddhist idea of 'the field of compassion': helping the poor plants merit.
Nothing is known about Gyōren beyond this section (so the 1925 edition).

notes.quote: 俗姓は三浦のなにがしとかや
notes.text: {俗姓|ぞくしやう}: the family name before he became a monk. The Miura were a powerful warrior family from the Miura peninsula, south of Kamakura. とかや: 'I believe'. {双|さう}なし: 'without equal'.

notes.quote: 吾妻人こそいひつることは頼まるれ
notes.text: {吾妻人|あづまうど}: people from the east, the provinces around Kamakura where the shogunate and its warriors were. To people in Kyoto, easterners were rough country warriors. こそ … るれ: the realis form of る, here 'can (be relied on)'.
{言受|ことう}け: saying yes, agreeing (the 1925 edition: 'consent'). Later in the section, ことうけしつ: 'they say yes'.

notes.quote: 乏しくかなはぬ人のみあれば
notes.text: The 1925 edition explains: 'poor, so they cannot carry it out even when they mean well'. The priest's argument is economic: the people of the capital are not false, only poor.
{心|こころ}の{色|いろ}: 'colour of the heart', tenderness. すくよか: 'stiff, blunt'. He is as blunt about his own people as they are.

notes.quote: 声うちゆがみあらあらしくて
notes.text: 'His voice was crooked and rough': the 1925 edition takes it as a country accent. Kenkō does not hide his first impression.

{心憎|こころにく}し: 'admirable, impressive' (see section 150). こそ earlier in the sentence (ことわられ侍りしこそ) never gets its closing form: the sentence runs on and ends in し instead of しか. That happens in long sentences.
